narrative:
The prediction system estimated a 69% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty of failure, but it means the model viewed failure as more likely than passing, and that risk estimate was high enough for your law school application to be rejected.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class-rank decile, which was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your third-year decile of 1 is far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, so this was the clearest academic signal behind the decision. Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA were the next most influential factors, but both were weaker and, in this prediction, leaned toward passing rather than failure. Your LSAT of 35 is below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and your GPA of 2.70 is below the 3.23 average; even so, they did not outweigh the third-year rank concern.

Next, request an individualized admissions review and ask how the bar-risk estimate was used. Provide context for the low third-year rank, such as grade trends, extenuating circumstances, or strong later coursework. Speak with a pre-law advisor about strengthening your academic record, consider LSAT preparation or retaking if appropriate, and discuss whether additional coursework or a revised school list would improve your chances.
